# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
#load all packages needed 
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Project Summary:

*Once you have completed this entire assignment, come back and write a project summary here that covers the aims, research questions, and basic methods of this study.*

In this project, the assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations are recorded among sites around Crystal Cove State Parks that are marine protected areas in Orange County. The owl limpet populations aim to determine if human visitation disturb the growth and if the sizes vary by year. In addition, as owl limpets can be territorial, this project records their territory size and determine if correlation occurs between its size and territory area. The methods of this study is to survey owl limpets by recording their sizes, habitats. To record the territory of owl limpets, a transect (0m-20m) will be placed with a mesh quadrat counting the number of squares to the nearest 0.5. To calculate the area of territory, the column of squares will be counted and multiplied with its counted width of the net. Using R Studio, the limpet data was imported along with packages of dplyr to organize the data set for statistical analysis and create figures, readxl to read excel sheets, and ggplot2 to create and summarize visual figures. The statistical analysis that was used in this project were anova, t-test, Shapiro-Wilk, and

You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

-   2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

-   2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

-   2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

-   2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

```{r}
SizeData_2022_2025
```

## Part 2: Population Density

For the population density analysis, we will analyze data from Shaws Cove, Heisler Park, and Treasure Cove. Create a data frame that excludes the Corona del Mar data, as that site did not have area measured.

```{r}
#loaded the data set and filtered out any "CDM" sites
No_CDM_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site != "Corona del Mar")
```

#### 2.1. How many limpets did we measure at each site in each year for sizes?

Use nrow(), group_by() and count() to tally the limpet observations at each transect. We used the same transect numbers at Shaws and Heisler, so group_by() site as well.

```{r}
#loaded the data to see below
No_CDM_Sizes

# How many did we measure total, across both sites?
#calculated the total of Shaws Cove and Heisler Park sites
No_CDM_Sizes |> 
nrow()
## How many did we measure at each site? 
#grouped the site and counted the number of rows 
No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(site) |> 
  summarise(count=n())
# How many did we measure in each transect? 
#count how many transect numbers were present in the data
No_CDM_Sizes |>
  group_by(site) |>
  count(transect_num)
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
#selected and combined the variables needed to calculate density then made a new column for density
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |>
  select(transect_length_m, site, transect_num, year) |>
  group_by(transect_length_m, site, transect_num, year) |> 
  summarise(count = n()) |>
#calculate the density and create a new column
  mutate(density = count/(transect_length_m*2))
#displayed the count and density in each site, transect length, and year
print(Limpet_Density)
```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

Treasure Cove displays a decrease in trend when it comes to organism count and density in the year 2023 and 2025.

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}
#calculated the mean of the densities
Limpet_Density$density |> 
  mean()
#calculated the standard deviation of the densities
Limpet_Density$density |> 
  sd()
#calculated the sample size of the densities
n <- Limpet_Density$density |> 
  length()
#calculated the standard error of the densities
Limpet_Density$density |> 
  sd()/sqrt(n)
```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations
#calculated the summary statistics for the density then grouped it by year and site then rounded to 2 decimal points
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |>
  group_by(site, year) %>% 
  summarise(mean_density = mean(density, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_density = sd(density, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n(),
            se_density = sd_density/sqrt(n)) %>% 
  mutate_at(vars(mean_density, sd_density, se_density), # bonus line to reduce digits
            .funs = round, 2) 

# Display your summary nicely using kable(). #created a organized table of all the variables calculated
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)
```

The data does not meet the assumptions for a t-test.

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

-   Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)?

    Numerical

-   Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population?

    Yes

-   Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)?

-   Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

    The data is skewed to the right due to some sites having higher limpet densities than the other.

#### 2.8 EXTRA CREDIT: Do an ANOVA comparing Shaws, Heisler, and Treasure Cove 2025 density data (exclude 2023 so that the sample size is similar between all three). Use a Tukey post-hoc test. Explain the results.

```{r}
#filter the data and rename a new data set
anova_density_data <- Limpet_Density |>
  filter(year == "2025" | year == "2024")
#display the data to make sure the filter is implied
show(anova_density_data)
#create a linear model from the dataset and the variables you want to test
model <- lm(density ~ site, data = anova_density_data)
#plot the anova density data to see the relationship between site and density
ggplot(anova_density_data) + 
  aes(x = site, y = density) + 
  geom_boxplot()
#create a QQ plot to see the standardized residuals from a fitted regression model 
plot(model, which = 2)
#create a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals 
shapiro.test(model$residuals)
#create a Bartlett test for density and site to see the homogeneity of variances 
bartlett.test(density~site, data=anova_density_data)
#create an ANOVA of the statistical model to test significance
anova(model)
#find which site is significantly different from each other after running the ANOVA test
TukeyHSD(aov(density~site, data = anova_density_data))
```

The Tukey test displayed a significant value of the relationship of limpet density and site between Treasure Cove and Shaws Cove with a value of 0.0058. The rest of the other sites do not display a significant difference in the relationship between limpet density and their sites.

#### 3.1 Summary Statistics

```{r summary statistics }
SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  group_by(site, year) |> 
  summarize(mean_shell = mean(shell_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_shell = sd(shell_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),

          mutate_at(vars(mean_shell, sd_shell, n),
```

```{r}
ggplot(SizeData_2022_2025) +
  aes(x = site, y = shell_length_mm, fill = year) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(y = "Shell Length",
       x = "Site",
       title = "Limpet Shell Length by Site")
```

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

-   Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

-   Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

-   Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
#create a dataset filtered with sites CDM and Treasure Cove
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site == "Corona del Mar" | site == "Treasure Cove")

# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
#create a linear model between shell length and site using the data created above
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
#plot the residual vs fitted between length and site
plot(model, which = 1)

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
#create a f test to compare shell length and site, this test also shows the p value and confidence interval
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

-   Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

    No because the distribution displays unequal data clumps on both ends. If the data was normal, the data would be distributed equally among the line of fit.

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
#create a normal quartile-quartile graph for a linear model object
plot(model, which = 2)

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
#create a Shapiro test to check if the data sample came from a normal distributed population
shapiro.test(model$residuals)
```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
#calculate a 1 sample t test for the size and shell length at CDM 
t.test(CDM_TC_Sizes$shell_length_mm)
#The t test tells us if the shell lengths are different enough to be statistically significant. 
```

```{r}
CDM_TC_Sizes |>
```

I am confident the t-test was drawn from different populations as it gives a small standard error. The standard error is small due to the similarities of the site. Also another possibility is the distance from each site making the owl limpet shell sizes similar from one another.

#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

-   territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

-   Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
#create new columns using the data set
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> 
#create a new column using the calculation for the area of limpet territory
  mutate(territory_area_mm = numbsquares*19*19) |> 
#create a new column using the calculation to find the limpet body mass
  mutate(body_mass = 0.00009*size_mm ^ 3.0471)
  # create a new column for territory area in mm^2 using the "numbsquares" column
         # mesh = 19 mm x 19 mm 

  # create a new column for limpet body mass
  # formula: mass_g = 0.00009*length ^ 3.0471

```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

```{r}
# write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 
#create a linear model from the dataset and the variables you want to test
linear_model <- lm(body_mass ~ territory_area_mm, data = All_Territories_area_mass)
#plot four graphs to check the linear regression in the statistical anaylsis
plot(linear_model)
```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval
#create a scatter plot of body mass and territory area in natural log, add line of best fit with no SE zone, and label the axis
All_Territories_area_mass |> ggplot() + 
  aes(x = log(body_mass), y = log(territory_area_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# write the linear model object and examine the residual and QQ plots
#create a linear model for the variables you want to use from the data set
log_model <- lm(log(body_mass) ~ log(territory_area_mm), data = All_Territories_area_mass)
#plot the fitted vs residuals for a fitted regression model
plot(log_model, which = 1)
#create a QQ plot to see the standardized residuals from a fitted regression model 
plot(log_model, which = 2)
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}
#create a linear model using a natural log of territory area and body mass from the dataset
All_Territories_area_mass.lm <- lm(log(territory_area_mm) ~ log(body_mass), data = All_Territories_area_mass)
#run a statistical summary on the data 
summary(All_Territories_area_mass.lm)
#separate the slope value from the fitted linear regression model
slope <- coef(All_Territories_area_mass.lm)[2]
#gives the numerical value from the slope
slope
#separate the intercept value from the fitted linear regression model
int <- coef(All_Territories_area_mass.lm)[1]
#gives the numerical value from the integer
int
```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**

As I explored a new aspect of the data, I wanted to find out the relationship between their habitat of and their shell length in the span of one year.

My question: How do owl limpet shell length differ between in a open habitat or a patch habitat in the span of one year?

The data is very interesting, the data displays that the higher owl limpet shell length are present in 2025 than 2024 for both habitats.

```{r}
#create a new data set with the columns you want to use for graphing
```
